title: Breaking And Entering: Karen Marks
summary: Karen Marks joins Lauren on Breaking And Entering to discuss Karen’s former RRR show, the underground 80s music scene in Melbourne, and what to expect from her premiere show.
transcript:
Karen Marks joined Lauren Taylor in the Triple R studio on 23 March 2023, ahead of her Melbourne Town Hall concert on 28 April. They discussed the rediscovery of Cold Café, Melbourne’s punk scene, her work as a band manager and her long creative partnership with Ash Wednesday.

Lauren: It’s such a pleasure to have you joining us again in the Triple R studios.

Karen: Always a pleasure, Lauren.

Lauren: You were with us, with Simon and also Michael Kucyk from Efficient Space, back in 2019, when the complete collection of your works came out via that label, Cold Café, the 1981 minimal wave recordings of Karen Marks. I think we discussed at the time you had a show on Triple R back in the day.

Karen: Oh, so long ago. It was, where was it? Cardigan Street, Carlton, I think, at the time. Midnight show it was. Ash used to come with me. I played very, very dirgy, depressing songs, which are my preference, of course.

Lauren: Do you remember what the show was called?

Karen: Music to Slash Your Wrists By, I believe.

Lauren: Your friendship with Ash dates back all that way as well. You’ve had a long-term friendship, which we’ll talk about, with Ash Wednesday. You’re going to be doing a one-off show at the Melbourne Town Hall, which is very exciting, where people can hear your tracks live for the very first time. But I wanted to talk through that track that we just heard. It was a reworking by a Japanese producer.

Karen: Well, so you told me. I’d never heard it before, and when it first went on, I thought it was me. I think it’s a bit of a case of spot the difference, because I really couldn’t spot much of a difference.

Lauren: I think that is you definitely singing.

Karen: Oh, it is. I don’t really know what they did to redo the song.

Lauren: It is quite similar. I loved hearing you talk that through off air. Listeners to Triple R in the ’80s would have been well aware of that single at the time. It was really an underground hit, especially on Triple R. It’s become a cult classic and recognised as one of Australia’s most popular minimal wave recordings, reissued by Efficient Space that we mentioned. I played that Hotaru edit because it does sound like such a contemporary song that fits into the landscape now. What’s it been like from your perspective, seeing the path that that track ‘Cold Café’ has taken over the years?

Karen: Well, it’s fabulous because it really didn’t do anything for many years. When we first released it, I think the minimal wave, if you like, market was very, or the alternative market, which is what I refer to it as at that time, was really, really small, and too small, really, for it to make much of a mark. I think Triple R had just started. I don’t even know whether PBS was around. I know it was number one on Triple R and triple j at that stage. But it was a very small market at that point. At the time, on reflection, I could easily have picked up and gone overseas where the market was larger. But I knew that really there wasn’t much for me here, musically.

It really just ran its course and then nothing, really, for many, many, many years, until this new generation of record fans and collectors and these new record companies, young, energetic people. The first I heard of it was from Michael Kucyk and his collaborators with the compilation album Sky Girl, which I think is terrific. I was contacted to do that and looked into it and said yes, and was quite surprised when it came out on vinyl and CD and it was released all over the world. Really, that was the start of this, and it did very, very well.

I think with the internet these days, it’s easy now for a young artist to get their product around the world and to find their market if it doesn’t exist where you live. A lot of time’s gone by, but it just got rereleased and hit a nerve or a mark where it fitted in to a lot of the things that are happening now. I’m thrilled about that. My support acts for the concert are fans of the song and of me, and that gives me a real kick. They’re young girls starting out and it’s fabulous. I feel really, really fantastic about that.

The song really started because of Michael Kucyk finding it, DJ Sundae and [Unclear audio at 00:05:47–00:05:51] in France. Then Michael asked me if he could put the four songs I recorded at that time out, which is when I spoke to you when that was released. Again, my followers are, I would say, largely overseas. But the market is huge now. It’s been a really fun journey, and I just feel for the song. I say to Michael quite often, if it wasn’t for you, it would just be in a drawer because I certainly wasn’t going to do anything with it. I’m very grateful for that and just think the whole thing is fabulous and fun, and a wonderful ride. It’s just got legs. It just keeps going, just keeps going. Then this idea of the concert was unexpected. Again, just another angle, another road to follow with the song. And here we are.

Lauren: Since we last had you on the show in 2019, there’s been a number of these local reissues and bands resurfacing from around that time. I’m thinking of Chapter Music rereleasing Essendon Airport’s first music.

Karen: They’re a cute little outfit. They’re always a really wonderful little outfit. I was sorry I missed that the other night. Did you go?

Lauren: I didn’t go. I missed that, unfortunately. They’re doing their first shows in a very, very long time, and it feels like there’s that resurgence of music from around that time. What is it that you feel like artists today are connecting with about that era specifically?

Karen: Well, I can’t really say. I just think music, in a way, is cyclical. You might get highly produced music for a while, and then people get sick of that, and then it goes back to being quite minimal. Really, let’s face it, there’s only X amount of chords. I believe that Ash was way ahead of his time here when we first recorded all of these songs. Now, of course, that’s a big, big, big market, electronic music. There’s festivals all over the world for electronic music, which I’d really, really like to pursue.

I think music connects always, really. It does go in cycles. We lucked out with just hitting the mark when we did, when we came back when we did. Again, as I said before, the population has grown so much larger that the market is larger now. The internet means that you’re not just relying on the market in Melbourne or the market in Australia. You’ve got the whole wide world.

Lauren: We’ve got a minimal wave legend, icon, Karen Marks joining us.

Karen: I love that, by the way. I’m using that.

Lauren: Go for it. Karen, I want to rewind and reflect on the time. You’ve described the ’70s and ’80s Melbourne music scene of your youth as a big family who would drive up and down Punt Road twice in one night, gig hopping from the Kingston Hotel in Richmond to the Tiger Lounge to Martinis in Carlton to the Crystal Ballroom. I was wondering for listeners if you could take us back there, set the scene, what brought you to that moment and your history in music?

Karen: Well, it’s quite a long story, so I’ll try and keep it short. It’s true that the rock and roll scene really was quite a small family, or really we did feel like a great big family, and all sorts of music went. We’d go to these venues, not really caring who was on, but everybody knew each other, and you’d know that you’d meet up with your friends. All of a sudden these young men appeared with black clothes, and they were punks, and they came and started mixing with us and sussing out what was going on. Then a couple of the venue owners put them on on a special night, the punks, and that was all starting.

To cut a long story short, I started managing The Boys Next Door, not for very long, but for a short time. I was approached by this band called JAB, which was Ash, Johnny and Bohdan, who had come from Adelaide. I said, well, I can’t really, I’m already managing The Boys Next Door. But they kept at me and then I stopped managing The Boys Next Door. That’s another story. Then I started managing them, and it became quite apparent that Ash and John were quite ambitious and quite serious about their music. It went from being a bit of fun to being, oh, we could really do something.

People were leaving the band and other people were added. Pierre [Unclear audio at 00:11:53–00:11:57] was added to JAB so that Ash could play synthesiser, and he started playing bass, Pierre. Then that evolved into Models, with Pierre, Ash and John. They auditioned people and got in Mark, who knew Johnny from Peter Lillie’s band. That was Mark Ferrie and Sean Kelly, who Pierre knew from Teenage Radio Stars. There were quite a few people that auditioned, and then they decided on them, and that became Models.

Ash and John and I really, it was Ash and John and I with the vision, I think, of where we wanted to go and that we wanted to take it further. Then there were some, what do you call them, artistic differences. Models got really, really, really, really big, really fast. We would find venues and fill them to the rafters, full houses by nine at night. We had a huge following. We were Triple R’s darlings. We did all of their functions and live to airs, and it was huge with Sean, Mark, Ash and John. I still think that was Models, really. Sadly, we never recorded. We were about to when the band fell apart. Ash and I left after a Sydney and Brisbane tour. Ash and I decided to leave because it wasn’t going the way that we envisaged it to go. Then Johnny left six months later.

But my relationship with Ash stayed. He was in a bit of a hiatus for a while. He had a studio in Brunswick Street, and we were really mucking around doing different musical things with his synthesisers and drum machines and things like that. Then that’s when we did this song. He ended up going over to Germany, thank goodness, where he was very, very, very successful, and ended up in, I can never pronounce it.

Lauren: Well, neither can I. I’m going to say Einstürzende Neubauten.

Karen: Einstürzende Neubauten, yes, which were, I went to see them at [Unclear audio at 00:14:20–00:14:23] a few years back when he came back, and I was just blown away. I thought they’d be a bit too avant-garde for me, but it was like art in motion. It was just extraordinary. Ash, because of medical reasons, ended up coming back to Australia a few years back now, and this is all happening. I wouldn’t be doing this without Ash, because I have no interest in doing music without him. We’ve just continued our musical journey together.

Lauren: It’s been a very important creative partnership for you. You’ve had a very, very long history with Ash Wednesday. I think there was that book called Dig, which Dave Nichols talks about Ash Wednesday as this technical wizard that specialises in obtuse ideas blended with an incredible sense of melody. Is that your view of Ash as well?

Karen: Well, I wouldn’t have said melody, but I definitely would have said obtuse. He’s just brilliant, really. He’s just, as I said, ahead of his time, extraordinary, very sensitive as well to other people’s music. He’s just a joy to work with. Anybody that’s worked with him finds him just to be such a wonderful human being and so clever and so open to other people. I’m a big fan.

Lauren: Karen, I did want to ask you about that time when you were managing bands like JAB and Models. You were one of only very few female music managers at the time. I think you mentioned that there was, is it Caroline Coon was managing?

Karen: Well, she was managing The Clash at the time, and I really don’t think there was anybody else. I know that female singers in the ’60s had women caretakers, if you like, or what do you call them? Chaperones. Some of my older musical friends could correct me if there was a female manager back then in the same ilk. But yes, that was problematic in a way when I was around. In another way, I found it incredibly easy.

I was interviewed once about all the problems and all the sexism, and really there wasn’t, except once a guy asked me for a kiss when he gave me our fee at the end of the night, which I laughed off. Didn’t give him one, by the way. Apart from that, I just felt, and also the boys protected me. I remember Johnny once, there was a bit of a run-in backstage somewhere and Johnny got very angry. See, I would have been working with John too, but sadly he passed away. I always think something’s three years ago and it’s about ten. I think ten now, Ash could correct me. But we’ve never really gotten over that. He passed away in Adelaide. He ended up back in Adelaide.

Being a manager, I think the music industry, which was full of men, only men, the rock and roll music industry, I think there was definitely a push to try and keep me out, which didn’t work. Definitely a push to not include me and not give me any credit. It is, and it was, and still is, incredibly sexist. They say that there’s women in the industry, but they always do the picking-up-the-pieces jobs. There’s no one really that’s got the spotlight jobs.

Lauren: You mentioned that your experience of punk was that it was the first time that women were allowed to play as well.

Karen: Well, yes, because I think I said in that [Unclear audio at 00:18:40–00:18:46], which Helen Marcou invited me to speak at, Why Punk, I think it was called. The speaker before me, who I won’t name, said that she found punk, all the boys really sexist, and I just didn’t. I actually think that punk was when women were able to pick up instruments and play with the boys. The Boys Next Door, I was their first manager. I was a woman. So I just don’t agree with that at all. I think the freedom that women then had musically, picking up guitars and singing and picking up bass guitars, I think it all really started then.

Lauren: It’s incredibly exciting that we now get to hear all of these songs live for the very first time.

Karen: And a couple more.

Lauren: I was going to ask about that. At Melbourne Town Hall on April 28, how did this live show come about? Did someone ask you to do it?

Karen: Miles Brown, who is the curator or manager, if you like, of all the instruments for the Melbourne City Council, including the magnificent grand organ at the Melbourne Town Hall, is an artist in his own right, a conceptual artist, musician, and a huge fan of Ash’s and a collaborator. Ash did a show there with the organ. Again, I can’t say how many years, two years, three years ago, audio, visual, sound, and it was recorded. I think they’re just polishing up the recording of it. Turns out to be a fan of mine as well. Then just a few discussions about this and that and whether we could do a show. I don’t have a film clip. Then the idea of doing a few European festivals came up, but we need some visuals and then maybe doing a gig. Miles suggested the Melbourne Town Hall, and I thought, I can’t fill the Melbourne Town Hall, but apparently everyone seems to think I can. So I thought, all right, then sure.

The next stage was that Ash and I have never performed this music with a band. That was always an interesting idea that we had. So we said to Miles, and Michael Kucyk, we would go into Bakehouse Studios, get a rehearsal space with select musicians and see if it worked. If it worked, we would say yes. If it didn’t work, well, that’s that. We did go in with Charlie Owen, Andrew Picouleau, Mal, I’m sorry, I don’t know his last name.

Lauren: Kilpatrick?

Karen: Yes, thank you. And Rick Hawkins, an old and dear friend of Ash’s and mine, who Ash has played with too before. It was really, really fabulous fun and worked really well. So we said yes, and then we picked a date. The publicity department for the Melbourne City Council like quite a long lead-up to do the publicity, so it was going to be February, but now it’s April the 28th. Sadly, Andrew Picouleau has got some health issues, so now he’s been replaced by Adam Learner, who I know of, but don’t know. We’ve got a series of rehearsals coming up. But yes, it’s taken the music into a whole different ilk, if you like, with the band. I’m looking forward to it, and I hope everyone else is too. So far, the response has been wonderful. There will be a couple of extra songs.

Lauren: Can you tell us a bit about those?

Karen: No. They’re going to be a surprise. There’s one cover and one of Ash’s songs added to the four.

Lauren: Incredible local support acts that you’ve got. You briefly mentioned earlier, but YL Hooi and Modal Melodies. I think YL Hooi are playing some brand new material as well. I can safely say that both of those acts would be very greatly honoured to be performing with you.

Karen: Michael, I think, and Miles were the ones that chose the support acts because I had another couple of ideas in my head, but they were already deciding that they would be really complementary. Then it turned out that actually [Unclear audio at 00:23:52–00:23:55] is a very close girlfriend of mine’s daughter. That’s lovely. That’s really nice that she’s going to be supporting me, and it’ll be a fantastic night that I’m looking forward to.

Lauren: You certainly paved the way for these artists and their sound as well. It’s going to be an incredible show. Very exciting to see Ash Wednesday, who’s, as you mentioned, utilising the venue’s 1920s-era grand organ.

Karen: That will be featuring in the concert.

Lauren: The track we’re about to leave on is Ash Wednesday and, I believe, yourself as well, ‘Love By Numbers’.

Karen: Again, this is something that we did in the downtime with Ash, which we did and released. This is really more of an indication of Ash’s more obtuse persuasion. Thanks very much for having me, Lauren.

Lauren: I believe this record that we’re about to hear from Ash is a career retrospective that’s received the vinyl treatment, coming out just in time for these live shows.

Karen: Yes, there’s a compilation of all of his works that will be released in time, and they’ll be able to be purchased on the night, along with a few other surprises.
